We denote by $Br(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})$ the category whose objects are the braided tensor functors from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{D}$ and whose morphisms are the natural tensor transformations.

Theorem XIII.3.7. For any braided tensor category $\mathcal{C}$ the functor $\Theta^{\prime}$ : $Br(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})\to \mathcal{C}$ defined by $\Theta^{\prime}(F)=F(1)$ is an equivalence of categories.

PROOF. By Proposition XI.1.5 again it is enough to prove that $\Theta^{\prime}$ is fully faithful and essentially surjective.

Full faithfulness of $\Theta^{\prime}$ . First, we claim that if $\mathcal{C}$ is a braided tensor category and F,F' are braided tensor functors, then

$$
\operatorname {H o m} _ {Y B (\mathcal {C})} \left(\Theta (F), \Theta \left(F ^ {\prime}\right)\right) = \operatorname {H o m} _ {\mathcal {C}} \left(\Theta^ {\prime} (F), \Theta^ {\prime} \left(F ^ {\prime}\right)\right).
$$

It is clear that the left-hand side sits inside the right-hand side. We have to prove the opposite inclusion. Let $f : F ( 1 ) = V \to F^{\prime} ( 1 )=V^{\prime}$ be an element of $\operatorname{Hom}_{{\cal C}}(\Theta^{\prime}(F),\Theta^{\prime}(F^{\prime}))$ . We wish to prove that f is a morphism in the category $YB({\cal C})$ , which means that the square (3.5) has to commute with $\sigma=\varphi_{2}^{-1} F(c_{1,1})\varphi_{2}$ and $\sigma^{\prime}=\varphi_{2}^{\prime-1} F^{\prime}(c_{1,1})\varphi_{2}^{\prime}.$ We have

$$
\begin{array}{l} (f \otimes f) \sigma = (f \otimes f) \varphi_ {2} ^ {- 1} F \left(c _ {1, 1}\right) \varphi_ {2} \\ = (f \otimes f) c _ {V, V} \\ = c _ {V ^ {\prime}, V ^ {\prime}} (f \otimes f) \\ = \varphi_ {2} ^ {\prime - 1} F ^ {\prime} \left(c _ {1, 1}\right) \varphi_ {2} ^ {\prime} (f \otimes f) \\ = \sigma^ {\prime} (f \otimes f). \\ \end{array}
$$

The second and fourth equalities follow from (3.12) whereas the third one follows from the naturality of the braiding c in $\mathcal{C}$

Now $\Theta^{\prime}$ is fully faithful in view of the isomorphisms

$$
\begin{array}{l} \operatorname {H o m} _ {B r (\mathcal {B}, \mathcal {C})} (F, F ^ {\prime}) = \operatorname {H o m} _ {T e n s (\mathcal {B}, \mathcal {C})} (F, F ^ {\prime}) \\ \cong \operatorname {H o m} _ {Y B (\mathcal {C})} \left(\Theta (F), \Theta \left(F ^ {\prime}\right)\right) \\ = \operatorname {H o m} _ {\mathcal {C}} \left(\Theta^ {\prime} (F), \Theta^ {\prime} \left(F ^ {\prime}\right)\right) \\ \end{array}
$$

where the first one follows by definition, the second one from the full faithfulness of $\Theta$ (Theorem 3.3), and the last one has just been proved.

Essential surjectivity of $\Theta^{\prime}$ . Let V be an object of C. Since C is braided, the automorphism $c_{V,V}$ is a Yang-Baxter operator by Theorem 1.3. According to Theorem 3.3, the functor $\Theta$ is essentially surjective, which means that there exists a tensor functor $(F,\varphi_{0},\varphi_{2}) : \mathcal{B}\rightarrow \mathcal{C}$ along with an isomorphism $\alpha:V\to F(1)$ such that

$$
\varphi_ {2} ^ {- 1} F \left(c _ {1, 1}\right) \varphi_ {2} (\alpha \otimes \alpha) = (\alpha \otimes \alpha) c _ {V, V}.
$$

(3.13)

(3.13)

In order to prove that $\Theta^{\prime}$ is essentially surjective, it is enough to prove that the functor F is braided, i.e., that for any pair $(n,m)$ of nonnegative integers the square $\left( C_{n,m} \right)$

$$
\begin{array}{l} F (n) \otimes F (m) \xrightarrow {\varphi_ {2}} F (n + m) \\ \Biggl < _ {c _ {F (n), F (m)}} \Biggr > \Biggl < _ {F \left(c _ {n, m}\right)} \Biggr ] \\ F (n) \otimes F (m) \xrightarrow {\varphi_ {2}} F (n + m) \\ \end{array}
$$

(3.14)

commutes. We shall check this by induction on n and m.

The commutativity of $( C_{0,0} )$ , $( C_{1,0} )$ and $( C_{0,1} )$ is left to the reader. Let us first check that $( C_{1,1} )$ commutes. We have

$$
F \left(c _ {1, 1}\right) \varphi_ {2} = \varphi_ {2} (\alpha \otimes \alpha) c _ {V, V} \left(\alpha^ {- 1} \otimes \alpha^ {- 1}\right) = \varphi_ {2} c _ {F (1), F (1)}
$$

by Relation (3.13) and naturality of the braiding c.

We now prove that the commutativity of $( C_{n,1} )$ and of $( C_{n,m} )$ implies the commutativity of $( C_{n,m+1} ).$ We have

\begin{array}{l} F \left(c _ {n, m + 1}\right) \varphi_ {2} = F (\mathrm {i d} \otimes c _ {n, 1}) F \left(c _ {n, m} \otimes \mathrm {i d}\right) \varphi_ {2} \\ = \varphi_ {2} \left(\mathrm {i d} \otimes F \left(c _ {n, 1}\right)\right) \varphi_ {2} ^ {- 1} \varphi_ {2} \left(F \left(c _ {n, m}\right) \otimes \mathrm {i d}\right) \varphi_ {2} ^ {- 1} \varphi_ {2} \\ = \varphi_ {2} (\mathrm {i d} \otimes \varphi_ {2}) (\mathrm {i d} \otimes c _ {F (n), F (1)}) (\mathrm {i d} \otimes \varphi_ {2} ^ {- 1}) \varphi_ {2} ^ {- 1} \\ \varphi_ {2} \left(\varphi_ {2} \otimes \mathrm {i d}\right) \left(c _ {F (n), F (m)} \otimes \mathrm {i d}\right) \left(\varphi_ {2} ^ {- 1} \otimes \mathrm {i d}\right) \varphi_ {2} ^ {- 1} \varphi_ {2} \\ = \varphi_ {2} (\mathrm {i d} \otimes \varphi_ {2}) (\mathrm {i d} \otimes c _ {F (n), F (1)}) a \left(c _ {F (n), F (m)} \otimes \mathrm {i d}\right) \\ \left(\varphi_ {2} ^ {- 1} \otimes \mathrm {i d}\right) \varphi_ {2} ^ {- 1} \varphi_ {2} \\ = \varphi_ {2} (\mathrm {i d} \otimes \varphi_ {2}) c _ {F (n), F (m) \otimes F (1)} a

\varphi_ {2} ^ {- 1} \varphi_ {2} \\ = \varphi_ {2} (\mathrm {i d} \otimes \varphi_ {2}) c _ {F (n), F (m) \otimes F (1)} a \left(\varphi_ {2} ^ {- 1} \otimes \mathrm {i d}\right) \varphi_ {2} ^ {- 1} \varphi_ {2} \\ = \varphi_ {2} c _ {F (n), F (m + 1)} (\mathrm {i d} \otimes \varphi_ {2}) a \left(\varphi_ {2} ^ {- 1} \otimes \mathrm {i d}\right) \varphi_ {2} ^ {- 1} \varphi_ {2} \\ = \varphi_ {2} c _ {F (n), F (m + 1)}
. \\ \end{array}

The first equality is a consequence of the fact that $(c_{n,m})_{n,m}$ is a braiding for $\mathcal{B}$ , the second one follows by the naturality of $\varphi_{2}$ , the third one by the commutativity of $(C_{n,1})$ and $(C_{n,m})$ , the fourth one by Relation (XI.4.1), the fifth one by Relation (1.3), the sixth one by naturality of the braiding in $\mathcal{C}$ , the seventh one again by Relation (XI.4.1).

A similar computation shows that the commutativity of $( C_{1,n} )$ and of $( C_{n,m} )$ implies the commutativity of $( C_{n+1,m} )$ . This is enough to prove that all squares $( C_{n,m} )$ commute. Therefore the functor F is braided and the proof of Theorem 3.7 is complete.

We may interpret Theorem 3.7 as saying that, given any object $V$ in a braided tensor category $\mathcal{C}$ with braiding $c$ , the tensor power $V^{\otimes n}$ of $V$ (whatever parenthesizing is used) is naturally a module over the braid group $B_{n}$ . If, moreover, $c_{V,V}$ is an involution, i.e., of square one, then the action of $B_{n}$ factorizes through the symmetric group $S_{n}.$

The proof of the essential surjectivity of $\Theta^{\prime}$ shows that the following more precise result holds for any strict braided tensor category.

Corollary XIII.3.8. Let $V$ be an object of a strict braided tensor category $C$. Then there exists a unique strict braided tensor functor $F_{V}$ from the braid category $B$ to $C$ such that $F_{V}(1) = V$.

## XIII.4 The Centre Construction

We now give a construction which assigns to any strict tensor category $(\mathcal{C},\otimes ,I)$ a braided tensor category $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$ , called the centre of $\mathcal{C}$ . When $\mathcal{C}$ is the tensor category A-Mod of modules over a finite-dimensional Hopf algebra A with an invertible antipode, then $\mathcal{Z}(A\text{-Mod})$ is tensor equivalent to the braided tensor category D(A)-Mod of modules over the quantum double D(A) of A, as described in Chapter IX. In other words, this "centre construction" is the categorical version of the quantum double construction.

Definition XIII.4.1. An object of $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$ is a pair $( V,c_{-,V} )$ where $V$ is an object of $\mathcal{C}$ and $c_{-,V}$ is a family of natural isomorphisms

$$
c _ {X, V}: X \otimes V \rightarrow V \otimes X
$$

defined for all objects X in C such that for all objects X, Y in C we have

$$
c _ {X \otimes Y, V} = \left(c _ {X, V} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {Y}\right) \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes c _ {Y, V}\right).
$$

(4.1)

A morphism from $(V, c_{-, V})$ to $(W, c_{-, W})$ is a morphism $f : V \to W$ in $C$ such that for each object $X$ of $C$ we have

$$
(f \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {X}) c _ {X, V} = c _ {X, W} (\mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes f).
$$

(4.2)

The naturality in Definition 4.1 means that the square

(4.2)

The naturality in Definition 4.1 means that the square

$$
\begin{array}{c c} X \otimes V \xrightarrow {c _ {X , V}} V \otimes X \\ \Biggl < f \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {V} \Biggr & \Biggl < \mathrm {i d} _ {V} \otimes f \\ Y \otimes V \xrightarrow {c _ {Y , V}} V \otimes Y \end{array}
$$

(4.3)

commutes for any morphism $f : X \to Y$ in $\mathcal{C}$.

It is clear that the identity $\mathrm{id}_{V}$ is a morphism in $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$ and that if f,g are composable morphisms in $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$ then the composition g o f in $\mathcal{C}$ is a morphism in $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$ . Consequently, $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$ is a category in which the identity of $(V,c_{-,V})$ is $\mathrm{id}_{V}.$

We now state the main theorem of this section.

Theorem XIII.4.2. Let $(\mathcal{C}, \otimes, I)$ be a strict tensor category. Then $Z(\mathcal{C})$ is a strict braided tensor category where

(i) the unit is (I,id),

(ii) the tensor product of $(V,c_{-,V})$ and $(W,c_{-,W})$ is given by

$$
(V, c _ {-, V}) \otimes (W, c _ {-, W}) = (V \otimes W, c _ {-, V \otimes W})
$$

where $c_{X,V \otimes W}: X \otimes V \otimes W \to V \otimes W \otimes X$ is the morphism of $C$ defined for all objects $X$ in $C$ by

where $c_{X,V \otimes W}: X \otimes V \otimes W \to V \otimes W \otimes X$ is the morphism of $C$ defined for all objects $X$ in $C$ by

$$
c _ {X, V \otimes W} = \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {V} \otimes c _ {X, W}\right) \left(c _ {X, V} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {W}\right),
$$

(4.4)

(iii) and the braiding is given by

$$
c _ {V, W}: \left(V, c _ {-, V}\right) \otimes \left(W, c _ {-, W}\right)\rightarrow \left(W, c _ {-, W}\right) \otimes \left(V, c _ {-, V}\right).
$$

PROOF. 1. Let $(V, c_{-, V})$ and $(W, c_{-, W})$ be objects in $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$. We claim that the pair $(V \otimes W, c_{-, V} \otimes W)$ defined in Theorem 4.2 (ii) is an object of $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$.

Indeed, it follows from the properties of $( V,c_{-,V} )$ and $( W,c_{-,W} )$ that $c_{X,V\otimes W}$ is an isomorphism in $\mathcal{C}$ and that $c_{X,V\otimes W}$ is natural in $X.$ We have to check Relation (4.1) for $c_{-,V\otimes W}.$ For all objects $X,Y$ of $\mathcal{C}$ we have

$$
\begin{array}{l} c _ {X \otimes Y, V \otimes W} = (\mathrm {i d} _ {V} \otimes c _ {X \otimes Y, W}) \left(c _ {X \otimes Y, V} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {W}\right) \\ = \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {V} \otimes c _ {X, W} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {Y}\right) \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {V \otimes X} \otimes c _ {Y, W}\right) \\ \left(c _ {X, V} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {Y \otimes W}\right) \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes c _ {Y, V} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {W}\right) \\ = \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {V} \otimes c _ {X, W} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {Y}\right) \left(c _ {X, V} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {W \otimes Y}\right) \\ \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {X \otimes V} \otimes c _ {Y, W}\right) \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes c _ {Y, V} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {W}\right) \\ = \left(c _ {X, V \otimes W} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {Y}\right) \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes c _ {Y, V \otimes W}\right). \\ \end{array}
$$

The first and fourth equalities follow from (4.4), the second one from (4.1), and the third one by (XI.2.3), i.e., by the naturality of the tensor product.

The first and fourth equalities follow from (4.4), the second one from (4.1), and the third one by (XI.2.3), i.e., by the naturality of the tensor product.

2. Let $f : (V, c_{- , V}) \to (W, c_{- , W})$ and $f^{\prime} : (V^{\prime}, c_{- , V^{\prime}}) \to (W^{\prime}, c_{- , W^{\prime}})$ be morphisms in $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$. We claim that so is $f\otimes f^{\prime}$. Let us check Relation (4.2) for $f\otimes f^{\prime}$. We have

\begin{array}{l} (f \otimes f ^ {\prime} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {X}) c _ {X, V \otimes V ^ {\prime}} = (f \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {W ^ {\prime}} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {X}) (\mathrm {i d} _ {V} \otimes f ^ {\prime} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {X}) \\ \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {V} \otimes c _ {X, V ^ {\prime}}\right) \left(c _ {X, V} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {V ^ {\prime}}\right) \\ = (f \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {W ^ {\prime}} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {X}) (\mathrm {i d} _ {V} \otimes c _ {X, W ^ {\prime}}) \\ \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {V} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes f ^ {\prime}\right) \left(c _ {X, V} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {V ^ {\prime}}\right) \\ = \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {W} \otimes c _ {X, W ^ {\prime}}\right) \left(f \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {W ^ {\prime}}\right) \\ \left(c _ {X, V} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {W ^ {\prime}}\right) \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {V} \otimes f ^ {\prime}\right) \\ = \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {W} \otimes c _ {X, W ^ {\prime}}\right) \left(c _ {X, V} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {W ^ {\prime}}\right) \\ \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes f \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {W ^ {\prime}}\right) \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {X}

\mathrm {i d} _ {W ^ {\prime}}\right) \\ \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes f \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {W ^ {\prime}}\right) \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {V} \otimes f ^ {\prime}\right) \\ = c _ {X, W \otimes W ^ {\prime}} \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes f \otimes f ^ {\prime}\right)
. \\ \end{array}

The first and fifth equalities follow from (4.4) and from (XI.2.3), the second and fourth ones from (4.2), and the third one from (XI.2.1).

Now it is clear that the tensor product is well-defined on the objects and on the morphisms of $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$ . It is functorial and satisfies all the required axioms because it already does so in the original category $\mathcal{C}$ . Thus, the category $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$ is a strict tensor category. We next show that it is braided.

3. Let us start by proving that $c_{V,W}$ is a morphism in $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$ . We have to check Relation (4.2) for $c_{V,W}$ , namely

$$
\left(c _ {V, W} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {X}\right) c _ {X, V \otimes W} = c _ {X, W \otimes V} \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes c _ {V, W}\right)
$$

for all objects X in $\mathcal{C}$ . We have

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left(c _ {V, W} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {X}\right) c _ {X, V \otimes W} = \left(c _ {V, W} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {X}\right) \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {V} \otimes c _ {X, W}\right) \left(c _ {X, V} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {W}\right) \\ = c _ {V \otimes X, W} \left(c _ {X, V} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {W}\right) \\ = \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {W} \otimes c _ {X, V}\right) c _ {X \otimes V, W} \\ = \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {W} \otimes c _ {X, V}\right) \left(c _ {X, W} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {V}\right) \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes c _ {V, W}\right) \\ = c _ {X, W \otimes V} \left(\mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes c _ {V, W}\right). \\ \end{array}
$$

The first and last equalities result from (4.4), the second and fourth one from (4.1), and the third one from the naturality of $c_{-,V}$

4. The morphism $c_{V,W}$ is invertible by definition and it is natural with respect to all morphisms of $\mathcal{C}$ , hence to those belonging to $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$ . In order for $c_{V,W}$ to qualify as a braiding, it has to satisfy both Relations (1.5) and (1.6). Now (1.6) follows from the hypothesis (4.1) and (1.5) from (4.4). Therefore the tensor category $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$ is braided with braiding $c_{V,W}.$

We give a universal property of the construction $\mathcal{Z}$ . For any strict tensor category $\mathcal{C}$ the functor $\Pi :\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})\to \mathcal{C}$ given by

$$
\Pi \left(V, c _ {-, V}\right) = V
$$

(4.5)

is a strict tensor functor. It is universal in the following sense.

Proposition XIII.4.3. Let F be a strict tensor functor from a strict braided tensor category $\mathcal{C}$ to a strict tensor category $\mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ . Suppose that F is bijective on objects and surjective on morphisms. Then there exists a unique strict braided functor $\mathcal{Z}(F):\mathcal{C}\rightarrow \mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C}^{\prime})$ such that $F=\Pi\circ \mathcal{Z}(F).$

PROOF. Let us first prove the existence of $\mathcal{Z} ( F )$ . For any object V of $\mathcal{C}$ we set

$$
\mathcal {Z} (F) (V) = \left(F (V), c _ {-, F (V)}\right)
$$

where $c_{-,F(V)}$ is defined for all objects $X$ in $\mathcal{C}'$ by $c_{X,F(V)} = F(c_{F^{-1}(X),V})$ Here $c_{-,V}$ is the braiding in $\mathcal{C}$. Relation (4.1) is satisfied because $F$ is a tensor functor. Therefore $\mathcal{Z}(F)(V)$ is an object in $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C}')$.

If $f : V \to V^{\prime}$ is a morphism in $\mathcal{C}$ , set $\mathcal{Z}(F)(f)=F(f)$ . Relation (4.2) is satisfied because of the naturality of the braiding in $\mathcal{C}$ . This proves that $\mathcal{Z}(F)$ is a functor. Clearly, $\Pi\circ\mathcal{Z}(F)=F$ . Let us now check that $\mathcal{Z}(F)$ is a braided tensor functor. It preserves tensor products because of (1.5) and (4.4). It also respects braidings. Indeed, we have

$$
\mathcal {Z} (F) \left(c _ {V, W}\right) = F \left(c _ {V, W}\right) = c _ {F (V), F (W)}
$$

which is the braiding of $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C}^{\prime})$

The uniqueness of $\mathcal{Z} ( F )$ is a consequence of the fact that it preserves braidings.

Applying Proposition 4.3 to the identity functor of a braided tensor category, we get the following result.

Corollary XIII.4.4. For any strict braided tensor category $\mathcal{C}$ there exists a unique braided tensor functor $Z$ from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$ such that $\Pi\circ Z=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{C}}.$

## XIII.5 A Categorical Interpretation of the Quantum Double

We relate the centre construction of Section 4 to the quantum double constructed in Chapter IX. This will give us a simple categorical description of the quantum double.

Let $A=(A, \mu ,\eta ,\Delta ,\varepsilon,S)$ be a finite-dimensional Hopf algebra with invertible antipode S. Under this hypothesis, we constructed a braided Hopf algebra $D(A)$ in IX.4. Let us recall that we have $D(A)=A^{*} \otimes A$ as a vector space, that the Hopf algebras $A$ and $(A^{\mathrm{op}})^{*}$ are Hopf subalgebras of $D(A)$ , and that the universal R-matrix is given by $R=\sum_{i} a_{i}\otimes a^{i}$ where $\{a_{i}\}_{i}$ is a basis of A and $\{a^{i}\}_{i}$ is the dual basis. Finally, in Theorem IX.5.2 we proved that a module structure over $D(A)$ is equivalent to a crossed bimodule structure over A.

We are ready to state the main theorem of this section.

Theorem XIII.5.1. For any finite-dimensional Hopf algebra A with invertible antipode, the braided tensor categories $\mathcal{Z} (A-Mod)$ and D(A)-Mod are equivalent.

We defined the centre construction only for strict tensor categories. But there is no difficulty in extending it to A-Mod. We start with two preliminary results before embarking into the proof of Theorem 5.1.

We defined the centre construction only for strict tensor categories. But there is no difficulty in extending it to A-Mod. We start with two preliminary results before embarking into the proof of Theorem 5.1.

Lemma XIII.5.2. Let $( V, c_{-,V} )$ be an object of $\mathcal{Z}(A\text{-Mod})$ and $\Delta_{V}$ be the map from V to $V\otimes A$ defined for all v $\in V$ by $\Delta_{V} ( v )=c_{A,V} ( 1\otimes v ).$ Then the map $\Delta_{V}$ endows the left A-module V with a crossed A-bimodule structure.

PROOF. Let $\Delta_{V}: V \to V \otimes A$ be defined as above. By convention, we write

$$
\Delta_ {V} (v) = \sum_ {(v)} v _ {V} \otimes v _ {A} \in V \otimes A
$$

(5.1)

for any $v \in V$. We call $\Delta_{V}$ the coaction of A on V.

The naturality of $c_{-,V}$ allows us to express $c_{X,V}$ in terms of the coaction $\Delta_{V}$ for any A-module X. Indeed, given x in X and $\bar{x}:A\to X$ the unique A-linear map sending 1 to x, we have the following commutative square:

$$
\begin{array}{l} A \otimes V \xrightarrow {c _ {A , V}} V \otimes A \\ \Biggl \downarrow_ {\bar {x} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {V}} \Biggl \downarrow_ {\mathrm {i d} _ {V} \otimes \bar {x}} \\ X \otimes V \xrightarrow {c _ {X , V}} V \otimes X. \\ \end{array}
$$

It implies that for any $v\in V$ and $x\in X$ we have

$$
c _ {X, V} (x \otimes v) = \Delta_ {V} (v) (1 \otimes x) = \sum_ {(v)} v _ {V} \otimes v _ {A} x.
$$

(5.2)

Let us show that the coaction $\Delta_{V}$ is coassociative. By (4.1) we have

$$
\begin{array}{l} c _ {X \otimes Y, V} (x \otimes y \otimes v) = \sum_ {(v)} v _ {V} \otimes \left(v _ {A}\right) ^ {\prime} x \otimes \left(v _ {A}\right) ^ {\prime \prime} y \\ = \left(c _ {X, V} \otimes \mathrm {i d} _ {Y}\right) \left(\left(\mathrm {i d} _ {X} \otimes c _ {Y, V}\right) (x \otimes y \otimes v)\right) \\ = \sum_ {(v)} \left(v _ {V}\right) _ {V} \otimes \left(v _ {V}\right) _ {A} x \otimes v _ {A} y. \\ \end{array}
$$

Setting $X=Y=A$ and $x=y=1$ ,we get

$$
\sum_ {(v)} v _ {V} \otimes \left(v _ {A}\right) ^ {\prime} \otimes \left(v _ {A}\right) ^ {\prime \prime} = \sum_ {(v)} \left(v _ {V}\right) _ {V} \otimes \left(v _ {V}\right) _ {A} \otimes v _ {A},
$$

which proves the coassociativity of $\Delta_{V}.$

which proves the coassociativity of $\Delta_{V}.$

We also have $c_{k,V} = \mathrm{id}_V$ because $k = I$ is the unit of the tensor category of $k$-modules. This implies $c_{k,V}(1 \otimes v) = \sum_{(v)} \varepsilon(v_A)v_V = v$ for all $v \in V$. This means that the coaction $\Delta_{V}$ is counitary. So far we have proved that the coaction $\Delta_{V}$ equips $V$ with a structure of right $A$-comodule.

Let us now express the fact that $c_{X,V}$ is A-linear. For $a\in A,v\in V$ and $x\in X$ we have

$$
a c _ {X, V} (x \otimes v) = c _ {X, V} (a (x \otimes v)).
$$

Replacing $c_{X,V}$ by its expression in $\Delta_{V}$ , we get

$$
\Delta (a) \Delta_ {V} (v) (1 \otimes x) = \left(\sum_ {(a)} \Delta_ {V} \left(a ^ {\prime \prime} v\right) \left(1 \otimes a ^ {\prime}\right)\right) \left(1 \otimes x\right).
$$

## XIII.7 Notes

Braided tensor categories were introduced by Joyal and Street [JS91a] [JS93]. They generalize the concept of a symmetric tensor category which appeared in the 1960's in the work of Bénabou [Bén64] and Mac Lane [Mac63], and was extensively studied in relation to algebraic geometry and algebraic topology (see, e.g., [Del90] [DM82] [KL80] [Mac63] [SR72]).

The content of Section 3 is taken from [JS93]. Lemma 3.5 is the analogue of Theorem XII.4.2 for braids. We found the example of crossed G-sets in [FY89]. Exercise 4 is from [JS93].

The centre construction of Section 4 is due to Drinfeld (unpublished), to Joyal and Street [JS91c], and to Majid [Maj91b].

# Chapter XIV Duality in Tensor Categories

In the previous chapter we defined braided tensor categories modelled on the category of braids. We now introduce a class of tensor categories modelled on framed tangles or ribbons. These are the so-called ribbon categories. Their definition requires the concept of duality. However, when duality is involved, formulas quickly tend to become obscure and complex. To overcome this difficulty, we present a graphical calculus in which coloured tangle diagrams represent morphisms of tensor categories.
